samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick student-count tiers with a $6 small tier and give the same reasons against per-lesson pricing. A is more specific about the switch for current teachers: the middle tier stays at $9, small teachers' price drops immediately, and large studios get 90 days' notice. A also gives a concrete way to check prices (ask 8 to 10 big studios what they would pay), though its 'more than about 4 leave' churn threshold doesn't hold up arithmetically. B handles cliff friction at the tier edges well, but it raises prices for 45% of teachers, which looks closer to a revenue grab than a fairness fix, and its plan for checking prices before committing is thinner. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers choose the same tiered model and use the 40/45/15 split. B does better on migration, giving a 90-day hold for large teachers, unchanged prices for the middle group and new features shipped before the price rises. B is also clearer that its prices are placeholders and offers concrete checks, such as interviewing 8 to 10 big studios. B's churn threshold is wrong, though: losing 'more than about 4' of the 135 large teachers would not make the $19 tier earn less, and A's testing advice covers tier cutoffs more than prices.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the same tiers with similar prices, explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse, and work through the 40/45/15 split. A edges ahead because its migration plan is more concrete, its sensitivity table shows what happens if large studios leave, and it suggests specific checks: interview 8 to 10 large studios and watch the first 90 days. B is more explicit about the downsides of its own pick (teachers archiving students to stay under a cap, and the middle tier's 33% increase), but its guess at what a large studio earns is an unchecked assumption. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend three per-teacher tiers at nearly the same prices, matched to the 40/45/15 split, and both explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse. B is better on moving the existing 900 teachers over: it gives a dated announcement, a 3-month hold and a longer 6-month hold for large studios, while A offers alternatives without picking one. B is also clearer about what it doesn't know and how to test the prices: it suggests talking to 8 to 10 large studios, watching churn for 90 days with a set threshold for cutting the Large price, and running a churn sensitivity table. A names the downside of the tiers more directly, though: teachers archiving students to stay under a limit, and the risk of raising the middle tier by 33%.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick per-teacher tiers at 12 and 30 students, explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse, and give similar prices. B does better on the move-over plan, with a 6-month timeline and what happens to each group, and on how to check the prices: churn thresholds, watching for teachers bunching just under 12, and calls with Pro studios. B has two flaws: it says everyone stays at $9 for 6 months but also that Starter teachers drop to $7 immediately, and its 15%-cancellation cutoff doesn't match its own numbers, since losing 15% of Pro teachers costs far less than the extra $13 each brings in. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend three tiers by active student count with similar prices. A does more of what the rubric asks: it gives a dated, group-by-group plan for moving the existing 900 teachers, checks its revenue and churn maths, and names concrete tests and trigger points for changing course, including clustering just under a tier limit, which is a real downside of tiers. B is solid and is the only one to use the 6-vs-55 comparison directly, but its migration plan is vaguer, it states that big studios are the least likely to switch as if it were fact, and its fallback revenue figure is a little off ($8,595, not about $8,800).
